content: The studies reviewed indicate a positive trend in improving VO2 max among participants in exercise groups. Specifically, moderate improvements were observed in VO2 max in individuals living with HIV who engaged in aerobic or resistance training. Participants in these studies were aged 18 to 66 years and exercised for 20–135 minutes, three times per week, over periods ranging from 6 to 52 weeks. Improvements in cardiopulmonary fitness were noted in individual trials, but meta-analyses were limited due to variability in reported outcomes. In trials comparing high-intensity aerobic exercise to moderate-intensity exercise, clinically important improvements in VO2 max were observed, though these findings were not statistically significant. Sub-maximal heart rate showed a trend toward improvement among exercisers compared to non-exercisers, with a reduction of approximately 10 beats per minute. However, heterogeneity in exercise interventions across studies likely contributed to variability in results. Strength outcomes were assessed in several studies, with nine out of ten trials reporting improvements in strength among exercisers compared to non-exercisers. Combined exercise and testosterone interventions showed a non-significant trend toward greater strength improvements compared to testosterone alone. Aerobic and resistance training were effective in improving body composition, including reductions in fat mass and increases in muscle strength. Aerobic training demonstrated a slight advantage in reducing total cholesterol and LDL levels, while resistance training was more effective in increasing muscle mass and reducing fat mass. Concurrent training improved VO2 max and reduced fat mass, but results were inconsistent for other metabolic markers. Inflammatory markers, such as hs-CRP, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-18, decreased following aerobic training, with IL-18 also decreasing after resistance training. No adverse effects were reported, and exercise interventions were deemed safe for individuals living with HIV, including those with HIV-associated lipodystrophy syndrome (HALS). Improvements in VO2 max, fat mass reduction, and muscle strength were observed, but evidence for consistent changes in lipid profiles and glucose metabolism remains inconclusive. Overall, exercise interventions, including aerobic, resistance, and combined training, appear to benefit cardiopulmonary fitness, body composition, and strength in people living with HIV. Further research is needed to establish the dose-response relationship and clarify the effects of exercise on cardiometabolic markers in this population.
